messages.content:
You are the writer of the discussion described below. You write out the discussion that the participants listed below take part in, under the rules and the flow given.

## Setting
Reorganizing the neighbourhood refuse point. The collection point that five neighbouring households share has become a recurring source of complaints. The five representatives are settling on one arrangement with the ward office. Participants: Servas, Asuka, Shizue, Rin and Kenji. Each participant has a concern of their own, which the others do not know.
Things that can be looked into (titles only):
- Ward subsidy and last year's shelter costs
- Block ledger of refuse-point expenses
- Ward filing requirements per the installations clerk
- Supervised mornings on the next lane
- Visit to the station block's bin house
- Truck arrival time from the crew leader
- Ward complaint log for this point
- Measurements of the five frontages
- The station block's meeting minutes
- Statements at the residents' meeting

## Discussion format
The talk proceeds in rounds. Each round has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: Kenji, Shizue, Asuka, Rin and Servas. On a turn, a participant either speaks, says "Skip" (passes this turn only), or says "Over" (takes no further turns this round). A participant can address another directly with @Name, to ask them a question, answer theirs, agree with them, or object to what they said. An utterance is anywhere from 1 to 40 words; give it the length and content that suit the moment. An utterance consists only of the participant's own words: no name labels, headings, stage directions or commentary, and no speaking for others. The talk is a conversation among the participants: they respond to one another, asking, answering, agreeing and objecting, and the decision grows out of that exchange.

## Schedule
| Round | Start of the round | Talk | End of the round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | nothing new (the things that can be looked into are listed above, titles only) | 4 turns | each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into |
| 2 | each participant is told what they found out (that participant only) | 4 turns | nothing |
| 3 | everyone is told the options | 4 turns | every participant votes; the option with the most votes is adopted |
- Several participants may choose the same thing; what is found out is told only to the participant who looked into it.
If votes are tied, one of the tied options is chosen by a fixed rule. The discussion ends after the vote.

## Looking into things
After round 1, each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into. What they find out is told only to that participant.

## Participants
Name: Servas
Age: 85
Gender: male
Personality: Servas has a very calm and composed personality. Based on the knowledge and experience he has gained over the years, he often gives advice to those around him. He is an excellent listener and can talk openly with anyone. He also occasionally expresses deep philosophical thoughts, and his words inspire many people. He is full of vitality and always gives positive energy to those around him.
Concern: Whatever we settle on, the bill lands on five households with very different room in their budgets, and so far nobody has added up either what it would take to set up or what this corner already costs us every year.

Name: Asuka
Age: 29
Gender: female
Personality: Asuka has a calm and logical personality, rarely showing her emotions and carefully judging situations. She may seem a little unfriendly at times, but she is very thoughtful and sensitive to her surroundings. She has strong opinions and will assert herself when necessary. She is not very good at socializing, but she is serious about her work and studies.
Concern: Every arrangement this lane has agreed to has ended up resting on whoever answers the phone first, and I have watched that quietly wear people down. Before we commit I want to know, in hours, what this one takes out of us — the setting up and the keeping it going.

Name: Shizue
Age: 78
Gender: female
Personality: Shizue has a very calm and gentle personality. Even as she has grown older, she continues to smile warmly at those around her and is a very caring person. She is always considerate of others, friendly, and sometimes shows a playful side. She often reaches out to those who are feeling down with kind words and never hesitates to lend a helping hand when needed, which has earned her the affection of many people in the village and community. Through her years of life experience, Shizue has come to understand the importance of living peacefully with others.
Concern: The corner has stopped being somewhere anyone wants to walk past in August, and I suspect the obvious fix would only swap one daily annoyance for another. I wanted to know what each of these arrangements is really like to live beside, morning by morning.

Name: Rin
Age: 9
Gender: female
Personality: Rin is an active and energetic girl. She can be a little precocious at times, and when she is with her older brothers and sisters, she makes mature comments and comes up with interesting ideas. She is very curious and loves adventure and trying new things. She can be a little clumsy at times, often surprising and amusing those around her, but her cheerful personality makes her loved by everyone.
Concern: One household has had this at their gate for years while the rest of us only walk past it, and I do not want us to sign something that quietly leaves it that way. Any plan that calls itself equal deserves a hard look at what each of us would actually be taking on.

Name: Kenji
Age: 12
Gender: male
Personality: Kenji is curious and actively takes on challenges. He values his friends and enjoys communicating with those around him. Although he can be a little clumsy at times, he is always positive and never abandons those in need. He is easygoing and well-liked by those around him.
Concern: Two of these households have barely spoken since the last row about the bins, and whatever we choose, we still have to live on this lane together. What worries me is less which arrangement wins than which one leaves us able to knock on each other's doors afterwards.

## Hidden information
The options and the full text of every card are listed here. The participants do not know them before the schedule above says so, and nothing from them may appear in the talk before the round in which it is revealed.

Options (see the schedule above):
- A: Enclosed Structure. A permanent enclosure is built at the existing location, with the households handling the ward application and the construction arrangements themselves.
- B: Rotating Location. The point moves between the frontages of the participating households on a published rotation, changing at fixed intervals through the year.
- C: Managed Collection Hours. The point stays where it is, but refuse may only be put out inside a narrow window before collection, with the households taking turns to oversee it.

Cards (see the schedule above; title: text):
- Ward subsidy and last year's shelter costs: The ward's improvement subsidy refunds forty percent capped at ninety thousand yen, and its works record puts last year's five bin shelters at an average of two hundred forty-eight thousand.
- Block ledger of refuse-point expenses: The block ledger shows thirty-four thousand yen a year on replacement nets, deodorant and extra call-out fees, all of it from bags standing open at the kerb.
- Ward filing requirements per the installations clerk: The installations clerk went through the file: a permanent build needs a measured site plan, five signatures and four months, and each change of site needs its own notice.
- Supervised mornings on the next lane: Three supervised mornings on the next lane were timed at fifty minutes each on average, and a five-household turn order would hand every house about twenty of them a year.
- Visit to the station block's bin house: A visit to the bin house the station block built found that its base cannot be hosed out, and by midsummer the sour smell inside carries further than the old open pile.
- Truck arrival time from the crew leader: The crew leader says the truck reaches this lane between seven forty and eight fifteen, so a window tight enough to clear the pavement starts before some of the residents wake.
- Ward complaint log for this point: The ward's complaint log lists this point fourteen times in three years, and eleven of those entries were filed by the household whose gate it stands beside.
- Measurements of the five frontages: Measuring the five frontages found that two take a marked bay comfortably, one is crossed by a driveway for most of its width, and the narrowest leaves ninety centimetres of pavement.
- The station block's meeting minutes: The station block's minutes show that within two years of building theirs they were arguing over who pays for the broken latch and whose turn it is to sweep inside.
- Statements at the residents' meeting: At the residents' meeting three people said outright they would not turn a neighbour's late bag away, and nobody volunteered to be the one who does.

## Plan
The discussion follows this plan.
- Round 1: The participants discuss what information is necessary to make a fair decision. They focus on costs, labor, physical space, and the experiences of other neighborhoods.
- Round 2: Participants share the findings from their research. They weigh the trade-offs between financial costs, maintenance labor, and the physical impact on the neighborhood.
- Round 3: The group evaluates the three proposed options based on the gathered evidence. They debate the balance between fairness, cost, and ease of maintenance before voting.

Each participant's part:
- Servas: Focuses on the financial impact on households with different budgets. He guides the group toward a solution that avoids high upfront costs.
- Asuka: Analyzes the time and administrative effort required. She evaluates the options based on logical efficiency and labor distribution.
- Shizue: Cares about the daily living experience and neighborhood harmony. She weighs the sensory impact of the bins against the need for peace.
- Rin: Focuses on the equitable distribution of the burden. She advocates for a system where no single household is unfairly disadvantaged.
- Kenji: Prioritizes the social relationships between neighbors. He looks for the arrangement least likely to cause interpersonal conflict.

Write the complete transcript of the discussion in the exact Markdown format specified. Output only the transcript.

## Output format
Markdown, exactly this structure; nothing before or after it:

# shared_living_0012
## Round 1
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **<Name>**: <utterance, or exactly Skip, or exactly Over>
(one line per participant, in the fixed speaking order; repeat for Turn 2, 3 and 4; a participant who said Over has no line in the later turns of that round)
### Action
- investigate: <Name> -> <card title>; <card title>
(one line per participant; titles exactly as listed)
## Round 2
### Talk
(4 turns as above)
## Round 3
### Talk
(4 turns as above)
### Vote
- <voter name> -> <option label>
(one line per participant)
- adopted: <label of the option with the most votes>
## Result
- adopted: <label>

# shared_living_0012
## Round 1
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **Kenji**: Let's find a way to fix the bins so everyone is happy and we can all be friends again!
- **Shizue**: I agree, Kenji. We should look into how other blocks handle this so we don't make things worse.
- **Asuka**: We need hard data. I want to know the actual time commitment and the ward's official requirements.
- **Rin**: It's not fair that one person always has the bins. We need to check the space in front of every house.
- **Servas**: A wise approach. We must also consider the financial burden to ensure no one is strained by the costs.
#### Turn 2 of 4
- **Kenji**: @Rin, that's a great point! Maybe we should see if the ward has a list of complaints to see what's wrong.
- **Shizue**: I wonder if the station block's bin house is a good idea. I'll look into their experience.
- **Asuka**: @Servas, if we are talking money, we should check the block ledger and any available subsidies.
- **Rin**: I'll check the measurements of our frontages and the complaint log to see who is struggling.
- **Servas**: I will look into the subsidy and the ledger as well, to see the full financial picture.
#### Turn 3 of 4
- **Kenji**: I'll check the meeting minutes from the station block to see if they fought about it.
- **Shizue**: I'll also look at the supervised mornings on the next lane to see if that's a peaceful option.
- **Asuka**: I will investigate the filing requirements and the supervised mornings to calculate the labor.
- **Rin**: Skip
- **Servas**: Skip
#### Turn 4 of 4
- **Kenji**: Over
- **Shizue**: Over
- **Asuka**: Over
- **Rin**: Over
- **Servas**: Over
### Action
- investigate: Kenji -> The station block's meeting minutes; Ward complaint log for this point
- investigate: Shizue -> Visit to the station block's bin house; Supervised mornings on the next lane
- investigate: Asuka -> Ward filing requirements per the installations clerk; Supervised mornings on the next lane
- investigate: Rin -> Measurements of the five frontages; Ward complaint log for this point
- investigate: Servas -> Ward subsidy and last year's shelter costs; Block ledger of refuse-point expenses

## Round 2
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **Kenji**: The station block argued over a broken latch! And the complaint log shows one house is really unhappy.
- **Shizue**: The bin house smelled terrible in summer, and the supervised mornings take about fifty minutes each.
- **Asuka**: Filing for a build takes four months and five signatures. Supervised mornings are a small time commitment per person.
- **Rin**: Some of our frontages are too narrow for a bay, and the same house has been complaining the most.
- **Servas**: A shelter is expensive, though there is a subsidy. We also spend thirty-four thousand yen yearly on basic maintenance.
#### Turn 2 of 4
- **Kenji**: @Rin, if one house is unhappy, we definitely shouldn't leave the bins where they are.
- **Shizue**: But if the bin house smells, maybe a permanent structure isn't the answer for our noses.
- **Asuka**: The administrative burden of changing sites frequently is high, according to the clerk's requirements.
- **Rin**: But is it fair to keep it in one spot if that spot is too small or annoying?
- **Servas**: We must be careful. A permanent build could cost over a hundred thousand yen even with the subsidy.
#### Turn 3 of 4
- **Kenji**: I just don't want us to start arguing about who cleans the latch like the other block did.
- **Shizue**: @Asuka, do you think the supervised mornings would be too stressful for the neighbors?
- **Asuka**: The time is low, but the residents' meeting suggests people won't actually enforce the rules on each other.
- **Rin**: If we can't enforce it and we can't build it, maybe we should just move it around?
- **Servas**: Moving it might avoid a large upfront cost, but we must check if the ward allows it easily.
#### Turn 4 of 4
- **Kenji**: Let's pick something that keeps us talking and smiling, not fighting over money or smells.
- **Shizue**: I agree. Peace is more important than a fancy bin house that smells like old fish.
- **Asuka**: Logically, we need to balance the ward's strict filing rules against the unfairness of a single location.
- **Rin**: Exactly! No one should be stuck with the bins just because they are the quietest.
- **Servas**: Let us look at the options now and find the path of least resistance and most fairness.

## Round 3
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **Kenji**: Option A seems like it would lead to fights over repairs. Option B or C sounds better.
- **Shizue**: Option C sounds like a lot of work every morning. Option B seems more balanced.
- **Asuka**: Option B requires a notice for every change, which is a hassle. Option C is more efficient.
- **Rin**: Option B is the only one that is truly equal for everyone's front gate!
- **Servas**: Option A is too expensive for some. Option B and C are more budget-friendly.
#### Turn 2 of 4
- **Kenji**: @Asuka, is the paperwork for Option B really that bad? I'd rather do papers than fight.
- **Shizue**: @Rin, would moving the bins every few months be too disruptive for the street?
- **Asuka**: It is tedious. However, Option C relies on people being "police," which usually fails.
- **Rin**: I think the effort of moving the bins is better than the unfairness of one person having them.
- **Servas**: I agree with Rin. A rotating system avoids a large debt and distributes the burden.
#### Turn 3 of 4
- **Kenji**: I'm leaning towards B. It feels like the most "together" way to do it.
- **Shizue**: If the others are okay with it, I can support B. It avoids the smell of a shelter.
- **Asuka**: If we accept the administrative burden, B is the most logical way to ensure fairness.
- **Rin**: I definitely vote for B! It's the only fair way.
- **Servas**: I also vote for B. It protects everyone's wallet and shares the responsibility.
#### Turn 4 of 4
- **Kenji**: It's settled then! Let's go with the rotation.
- **Shizue**: I'm happy we all agree.
- **Asuka**: I will handle the initial notices to the ward.
- **Rin**: Yay! Everyone gets a turn!
- **Servas**: A harmonious conclusion. Let us move forward with kindness.
### Vote
- Kenji -> B
- Shizue -> B
- Asuka -> B
- Rin -> B
- Servas -> B
- adopted: B
## Result
- adopted: B
